A municipal water-distribution system is a pressurized, branched network of pipes, pumps, valves, reservoirs, and tanks that delivers potable water from treatment works and sources to homes, businesses, fire hydrants, and industrial users. What distinguishes a distribution system from a simple collection of pipes is that it must simultaneously satisfy three obligations: deliver adequate pressure at every point of use, preserve water quality from source to tap, and do so economically while accommodating demand that varies by location and by hour of the day. The physics is governed by conservation of mass and conservation of energy (expressed in water-supply practice as head loss), and the engineering response to those physics is the coordinated use of gravity, pumps, storage, valves, monitoring, and maintenance. This guide develops those themes in order: the physical basis, the role of gravity and elevation, pumping and head addition, storage and demand buffering, transient (water-hammer) behavior, leak detection and non-revenue water, water-quality protection within the network, and sensor placement and telemetry. It closes with operational integration—how the pieces are managed together as a system rather than as isolated components.

## 1. Physical Basis: Conservation of Mass and Head Loss

Two conservation principles anchor all distribution-system analysis. Conservation of mass, applied at each junction (node), requires that inflow equals outflow plus any demand drawn at that node; for a network of *N* nodes and *L* links, this yields *N* continuity equations. Conservation of energy, applied along each pipe, requires that the energy grade line (EGL) falls in the direction of flow by an amount equal to friction and minor losses. This review evaluates the design of an islanded electrical microgrid intended to serve a remote island community with no interconnection to a mainland grid. The generation portfolio comprises photovoltaic (PV) arrays, wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and dispatchable backup generators (typically diesel or dual-fuel). The central design constraint is that supply and demand must balance at every instant: the microgrid has no infinite bus to absorb surplus or make up deficit, so imbalance manifests immediately as frequency and voltage deviation.
